sources.title: "ADA YONATH", Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009, NobelPrize.org 'Women who changed science' series -- the Nobel Foundation's own biographical account, including her directly quoted self-testimony. Fully read in this cycle.
"Ada E. Yonath -- Facts", Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009, NobelPrize.org -- used to independently confirm birth/death dates and affiliation. Fully read in this cycle.

"'To Understand the Principles of Life': The Journey of Prof. Ada Yonath from Ribosomes to the Nobel Prize", American Committee for the Weizmann Institute of Science, feature story. Fully read in this cycle.

Max Barnhart, "Ada Yonath, Nobel laureate and crystallographer, dies at 87", Chemical & Engineering News (American Chemical Society), 1 Sep 2026 -- contains named, firsthand, non-self quotes from her 2009 Nobel co-recipient Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and from her former PhD student/postdoctoral mentee Miri Krupkin (Stanford University). Fully read in this cycle.

"Ada Yonath, chemist and first Israeli woman to receive a Nobel, dies at 87" -- obituary originally published by The New York Times, republished by Texarkana Gazette, 2 Sep 2026. Fully read in this cycle.

persistence.rationale: Three independently-read sources converge on the same specific, quantified facts: NobelPrize.org's own account states she "took on a challenge that others considered hopeless... and persevered for decades," specifically citing roughly 25,000 crystallization attempts before her first success in the early 1980s; the Weizmann Institute's own feature independently confirms the same 25,000-attempt figure across roughly two decades; the New York Times obituary independently confirms "a process of over 25,000 painstaking experiments" running from 1970 (when she founded Israel's only protein-crystallography lab) through the 1980s-90s refinement period. The extreme score is justified by this specific, quantified, multiply-corroborated duration and repetition count -- not by her eventual Nobel recognition.

experimentation.rationale: Two independently-read sources document a specific, unconventional methodological choice: rather than standard model organisms, she deliberately sourced ribosomal material from extremophile bacteria (thermophilic/halophilic strains, including some from the Dead Sea, and Geobacillus/Bacillus stearothermophilus) on the specific reasoning that hardier ribosomes would crystallize more reliably (NobelPrize.org, Weizmann Institute feature) -- then, working with Hakon Hope and Joel Sussman in the late 1980s, pioneered cryo-bio-crystallography (flash-freezing crystals at roughly -185C during X-ray exposure) specifically to solve the resulting radiation-damage problem, a technique the Chemical & Engineering News obituary independently confirms she then 'evangelized,' helping popularize it as a now-standard structural-biology procedure. A named, dated, technically specific innovation, not an inference from the eventual prize.

independent_thinking.rationale: The Weizmann Institute's own account and the Chemical & Engineering News obituary both independently document that, starting in the 1970s, she pursued ribosome crystallization after -- and despite -- named major laboratories (UCLA, MIT, the UK Medical Research Council) having already tried and abandoned the problem since the 1960s: an objectively documented pattern of institutional abandonment, not merely her own claim of having been doubted. Independently corroborated, non-self, by her eventual Nobel co-recipient Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, quoted by name in C&EN: 'By showing that you could get 3D crystals of the large subunit... she broke a very important psychological barrier to solving what seemed like an impossible problem.'

leadership_drive.rationale: The New York Times obituary documents that from 1986 to 2004 she ran two parallel ribosome-research units simultaneously -- her existing laboratory at the Weizmann Institute, and a second unit at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg, Germany, secured with Heinz-Gunter Wittmann's help -- commuting between the two countries for 17 years to oversee both teams; the Weizmann Institute's own feature independently confirms both units were 'headed by Prof. Yonath.' A specific, sustained, dual-institution leadership arrangement, not an inference from her later single-lab reputation.

collaboration.rationale: Miri Krupkin, who completed her PhD under Yonath and is quoted by name in the Chemical & Engineering News obituary -- a non-self, independent, firsthand account -- describes a specific mentoring pattern: Yonath 'would often spend 24 h shifts helping her students when they managed to get beam time reserved at a synchrotron,' and that even as a young trainee Krupkin 'felt from the first moment that she respected me as a full-grown scientist.' A concrete, named, first-person account of a specific working practice, not a generic reputation claim.

competitiveness.rationale: Two independently-read sources corroborate a real competitive dynamic: C&EN documents that 'the mid-1990s saw a race brewing to fully map out the ribosome, with many rivals participating,' and the New York Times obituary independently confirms that 'other researchers -- notably Venkatraman Ramakrishnan... and Thomas Steitz -- entered the field' around the same time, with all three efforts culminating separately before being jointly recognized. Scored dual_edged and at moderate confidence: the same sources show this resolved into genuine collegial respect rather than lasting antagonism (Ramakrishnan's on-record praise, quoted above), so this is scored as a real but non-adversarial competitive drive, not assumed hostility.

provenance.notes: LIVING-STATUS CORRECTION (this cycle, verified before any scoring): the task brief's working assumption (that Yonath might still be living) does not hold -- she died on 31 August 2026, per direct live verification of https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7426 (P570 death date 2026-08-31, referenced there to both an Israeli Ynet article and a French Le Monde obituary dated 1-2 Sep 2026, and corroborated by more than a dozen independent Wikidata language-editors updating descriptions to '(1939-2026)' within days of each other) and independently re-confirmed via the live NobelPrize.org 'Facts' and 'Women who changed science' pages (both now state 'Died: 31 August 2026' / 'Ada Yonath passed away on 31 August 2026'), the live English Wikipedia summary ('was an Israeli crystallographer...'), and two independently-read press obituaries (Chemical & Engineering News, 1 Sep 2026; New York Times, republished by Texarkana Gazette, 2 Sep 2026). identity.isLiving is therefore false and identity.deathYear is 2026, both against the brief's own stated assumption -- flagged explicitly per this project's instruction that live repository/tool state overrides any cached or assumed claim. Portrait reuse verification (before any new research): the previously-downloaded local file public/portraits/ada-yonath-weizmann-2009.jpg (1591x1600) was independently re-verified against the live Wikimedia Commons API. Its aspect ratio (1591:1600 = 0.99438) matches, to within rounding of a 1600px-long-edge resize, the original Commons file 'File:Ada Yonath Weizmann Institute of Science.jpg' (2362x2375 = 0.99453; 2362 * 1600/2375 = 1591.1, rounds to 1591). The Commons API confirms this file's licensing directly: CC BY-SA 3.0, Credit 'Miki Koren, Weizmann Institute of Science' (via hayadan.org.il, the Israeli Weizmann-affiliated science-news site), AttributionRequired: true, dated 2009-10-08 (the week after her Nobel announcement), sha1 d9fb1ba958869ce51af2cf1661afcb25667a8254. Visually confirmed via direct image inspection: the local file shows Yonath at X-ray crystallography equipment in her lab, consistent with the documented source. Reused as-is; not re-downloaded. Research actually read in full this cycle (Wikipedia used only for orientation, never as a scored source): both NobelPrize.org pages; the Weizmann Institute's American Committee feature story; the Chemical & Engineering News obituary (with named non-self quotes from Ramakrishnan and Krupkin); and the New York Times obituary (via Texarkana Gazette). This gives 4 independent organizational perspectives (Nobel Foundation; Weizmann Institute; American Chemical Society/C&EN; New York Times) plus two genuine non-self, firsthand behavioral witnesses quoted by name (Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, her Nobel co-recipient and one-time scientific rival; Miri Krupkin, her former PhD student), well beyond this project's minimum provenance-diversity bar. A 6-row profile was judged the honest stopping point: every row traces to a specific, dated, quantified incident or named methodological/administrative fact, not to her fame or the Nobel Prize itself. Deliberately did not score a row from her documented public political statements (on the 2009 Gilad Shalit hostage situation and the 2023 Israeli judicial-reform debate, both reported in the C&EN obituary) -- out of scope for the specific scientific-persistence/collaboration/mentorship behavior this research was scoped to, and consistent with this roster's standing zero-politics-primary composition guidance. No promotion readiness or eligibility_v2 computation was run as part of this pass.
